The method extends the concept of radiance fields to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery [S1].

The claim states that the method extends the concept of radiance fields to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery. Source [S1] explicitly introduces 'Radar Fields' as a 'new framework for learning a volumetric model based on multiple SAR measurements' and describes it as a 'differentiable rendering framework that extends radiance fields to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images'. The source further details how this extension works by adapting the integration process (across rays in an azimuth plane rather than along individual rays) and the surface model representation, confirming that the evidence fully supports the claim.
supported
The method primarily focuses on intensity images, but phase contains satellite-target path delay modulo the wavelength [S1].

The claim consists of two parts: 1) The method primarily focuses on intensity images, and 2) phase contains satellite-target path delay modulo the wavelength. The evidence explicitly states in Source [S1] notes and passages that 'SAR raw data stores complex numbers separating amplitude and phase... while phase contains satellite-target path delay modulo the wavelength.' Furthermore, the evidence describes the method's focus on 'intensity images' (e.g., 'For single-channel single-look intensity images... the sample covariance matrix reduces to intensity I') and notes that 'Traditionally in SAR simulation... the intensity of the reflected signal is characterized by the surface.' While the method uses complex raw data, the rendering model and optimization described in the text heavily rely on intensity-based metrics and models (like the Lambertian/specular intensity model). Thus, the facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

"""Compute loss based on multiplicative speckle noise model [S1]."""

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and passages that for single-channel single-look intensity images, the noise-free reflectance R is modeled as I = n * R where n follows a Gamma distribution (Gamma(1, 1)). This is the definition of a multiplicative speckle noise model. The claim accurately reflects this modeling approach described in the source.

This involves evaluating the density $\sigma_{i,j}$ and normal $n_{i,j}$ at the intersection point, and applying the reflection model [S1]:

The claim states that the method involves evaluating density ($sigma_{i,j}$) and normal ($n_{i,j}$) at the intersection point and applying the reflection model [S1]. The provided evidence explicitly supports this in Source [S1] passages. Specifically, Equation (13) is given as $s(d_i) = -T_{i,j} sigma_{i,j} <v_j | n_{i,j}>$, which shows the evaluation of density and normal. Additionally, the text describes the reflection model $s = -<v|n>^theta$ (Equation 12) and notes that this parameter can be learned alongside surface location. The notes also confirm that integration is performed across rays for a given azimuth plane, consistent with the context of the claim.

All rays of a given azimuth plane must be batched together during computation [S1].

The claim is directly supported by the text in Source [S1]. Specifically, the notes state: 'Batch all rays of a given azimuth plane together during computation. This is necessary because computing a single pixel requires computing all rays in that azimuth plane.' Additionally, the passage text confirms: 'In practice the only difference is how rays are batched. While there is no requirement in the radiance field case, it is necessary to batch all rays of a given azimuth plane together during computation for radar fields.'
supported

Unlike optical radiance fields that integrate radiance along individual rays, Radar Fields integrates radar signal contributions across all rays within a given azimuth plane that share the same range distance [S1].

The claim states that Radar Fields integrates radar signal contributions across all rays within a given azimuth plane that share the same range distance, unlike optical radiance fields which integrate along individual rays. The provided evidence explicitly supports this in multiple places: 1) The notes state 'integration is performed across rays for a given azimuth plane rather than along rays as in optical images.' 2) The notes define the total signal for a pixel at distance di as the sum over all rays in the azimuth plane. 3) The passages state 'the integration is performed across rays for SAR images and not along rays as in optical images: for a given azimuth, reflectors that are at the same distance are projected into the same pixel.' 4) Figure 1 description confirms 'radar fields integrates across rays (in red) in a given azimuth plane' while optical fields integrate along each ray.
supported
